All-Electric Porsche 718 Boxster Coming Out in Early 2027, Here's What It Brings
23 photos
Photo: Porsche
German carmaker Porsche is planning to start the new year with a hell of a bang. Sometime in the first three months of 2027, it will unveil the production version of its first all-electric two-door sports car, the new 718 Boxster.
Although in most ways that matter the new vehicle is based on the 911, its electric powertrain required some innovative thinking, especially in the way it is designed and integrated into the car. Why so? Well, for the simple reason that Porsche wanted the 718 to retain its mid-engine driving dynamics and low seating position, despite the fact that there is now no actual engine to speak of.
The carmaker calls the solution the E-Core, and it's been in the news, on and off, for about five years already. For the purposes of its use in the 718, it translates to the placement of the battery pack directly behind the car's two seats, the location where Porsche usually mounts some of the internal combustion engines it still uses.
Putting the 800-volt battery there allows the driver's seat height to be kept as low as required from a sports car, while at the same time making sure the bulk of the vehicle's weight is kept towards the middle.
There is talk of a 40 percent front and 60 percent rear weight distribution - a total weight that's not fully disclosed yet, but is similar to the present-day 911 Cabriolets that employ the T-Hybrid powertrain. In numbers, that could be anywhere between 3,693 pounds (1,675 kg) and 3,990 pounds (1,810 kg).
Photo: Porsche I said earlier that the new 718 Boxster is heavily based on the 911, and that is more obvious than anywhere when talking about the chassis components: steering, including, for the first time on this model, rear-axle steering, braking system, and even the electronically controlled limited-slip differential.
What is not derived from tech used on the 911 is, aside from the purpose-made E-Core solution, the vehicle's electric powertrain. Porsche does not go into the specifics of what that means, yet, but it does talk about an acceleration time from zero to 62 mph of under three seconds for the top-of-the-range model, and top speeds of 155 mph (250 kph).
We don't know at the moment how many versions of the electric car will be available, but Porsche confirmed that all of them will be rear-wheel drive and, on top of everything, will be equipped with something called the E-Shift.
It's a term you may be familiar with since the summer of this year, when the 2027 Taycan broke cover. Essentially, we're dealing with a virtual gearbox, more specifically the seven-speed PDK transmission that would normally be used in an ICE vehicle.
Photo: Porsche What the tech does is allow the driver to choose between automatic gear changes or manual shifts, achieved by using the paddles placed behind the steering wheel. For the purpose of tricking the senses, when the car is in E-Shift mode (people can choose not to enable it), the 718 also replicates the sounds of a six-cylinder boxer engine makes when shifting gears.
It's a lie, true, but a beautiful one, as the car whose sounds it replicates is none other than the 981-generation Boxster GTS .
I said earlier that people can choose not to enable this make-believe feature, and when that happens, the steering wheel paddles can be used to select one of three stages of energy recuperation.
We know all of these new details because Porsche shared them this week under the guise of an announcement detailing the extensive testing program the electric 718 Boxster has been subjected to. And this program is equally as impressive as the car itself.
Photo: Porsche The Germans claim to have traveled close to 2.5 million miles (four million km) with test vehicles, subjecting them to temperatures as low as minus 22 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 30 degrees Celsius) in Sweden and as high as 124 degrees Fahrenheit (51 degrees Celsius) in Death Valley.
Test 781s (unclear how many of them) covered the miles above both in the wild and in very crowded cities like Las Vegas , Los Angeles, and Shanghai, from as low as 279 feet (86 meters) below sea level to 9,022 feet (2,750 meters) above it, traveling in the process to some 20 countries.
Most of this journey has been documented on film and uploaded online so that we all can get a glimpse of what it meant. You can find the first episode of the documentary, called " The new 718 Boxster: a development story," attached below this text.
Porsche describes the new, electric 718 Boxster as an entry-level vehicle to its range of two-door sports cars. It will assemble it at the main facility in Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen, with the lines expected to start rolling soon. We will keep an eye on things and report back once we know more about the newcomer.
